What's new in 2.39.0

Forty-six changes, nearly all of them in Shepherd. The theme is knowing where you are: panes name themselves after the work in them, colour tells folders apart, ⌘J leads with the agent you were just in, and a pane can be picked up and put down somewhere else.

Every pane says what it is doing

  • A pane is named after the work in it, in a few words, read off the pane itself by Apple's on-device model. An agent writes its terminal title once, from the first thing you asked it, so a herd left running all afternoon was a list of names for conversations that ended hours ago.
  • Nothing leaves your Mac — the reading is done on the device, and a pane you have named yourself keeps your name. Without Apple Intelligence, panes keep the titles they always had. It can be turned off in Settings.
  • A shimmer sits where the rest of the name is coming, so a name that is still being read looks like it is arriving rather than like it stopped halfway.
  • A tab is named for the folder it is working in, and an agent's row says which folder it is in — so two checkouts of the same repo stop looking like the same place.

Colour tells folders apart

  • Every tab in a folder shares that folder's colour. Two folders means two colours, however many tabs are open in them — the tree, the collapsed strip, the tab bar, the flock and the Agent Monitor all follow at once.
  • Settings › Appearance › Colour chooses, with a small drawing of each scheme so the choice shows its work: one folder split three ways, against two folders held together. Each tab is still there for anyone who keeps one checkout with several tabs in it.
  • The folder's own row wears its colour too. A scheme that colours a folder's tabs and leaves the folder grey has left the label off the group it just drew.

Getting around

  • ⌘J leads with where you have lately been. Under the agents that have stopped for you and the ones still working, the rest of the list is now the order you last had things open — so bouncing between two agents is one keystroke each way instead of a hunt. Landing anywhere is remembered, not just a jump.
  • ⌃Tab steps through agents, not past them. A folder with four agents in two tabs used to answer two presses and move on, leaving most of the herd unreachable from the keyboard.
  • ⌘L can be typed into, so the machine you want is one word away, and ⌘K names the agent on a pill and opens with it.
  • One pair of buttons opens or shuts the whole herd, sitting on the first folder's row where your eye already is.

Panes you can pick up

  • Drag a pane onto another and they swap places. The tile takes the hand, the hand stays closed while you carry it, and opens again when you let go.
  • Drop a file onto a pane and its path goes to the agent in it. The drag is coloured by that pane's own sheep, a local drop gets a receipt, and a drop bound for a server is held while the network does its work rather than lost.
  • Paste a picture into a pane on a server and get a link back. ⌘V carrying a screenshot used to paste nothing at all — there is no text on the board, so the terminal inserted an empty string and said nothing about it. Herds on your own Mac are untouched: the file is already somewhere the agent can read it.

Servers

  • Open a folder on a server without touching the mouse — arrows walk the list, ↩ goes in, ← climbs, and the keys are named on the panel.
  • A connection test leads with a ring and keeps its log a click away, and deleting a server now actually comes off it rather than leaving what was holding it open.
  • A connection no longer waits on a pipe that ssh's background master will never close.

Files, and the pointer

  • ⌘E answers the pointer properly: a hand over a file, a caret in the search box, an arrow everywhere else. The browser is drawn over a live terminal, and the terminal was claiming the text cursor for the whole panel.
  • The search boxes can be clicked into and have a caret of their own.

Toasts, and coming back

  • Dax greets you rather than playing the intro again. The intro is for the first time; coming back gets a greeting, for as long as you set it.
  • An agent's card holds for five seconds, or whatever you set — there is a slider for it now. The countdown ring moves with the screen and eases at both ends, and a long toast title is cut in the middle rather than run off the edge.
  • An ordinary launch opens nothing at all, instead of putting a window in front of you that you did not ask for.

Also in this release

  • Dax keeps its own book of the herd, so a pane that comes back empty can offer itself back rather than sitting there dead.
  • The first-agent list says what the machine already has, and ↩ presses Start once an agent has finished installing.
  • A pane's uploads are counted as Image to URL and File Drop, and a dropped usage event now says so and names where it came from.
  • Signed, notarized, universal (Apple Silicon & Intel), macOS 14+.
